content: RICTOR, or Rapamycin-insensitive companion of mammalian target of rapamycin, is a protein encoded by the RICTOR gene in humans. This protein, along with mTOR, forms part of a protein complex that integrates signals derived from nutrients and growth factors to regulate cellular growth. The RICTOR gene spans 5440 base pairs and is located on the minus strand. The translated RICTOR protein consists of 1709 amino acids and is localized in the cytosol. RICTOR contains relatively few conserved regions, and its functional domains remain largely uncharacterized. However, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry analysis has identified 21 phosphorylation sites on RICTOR. Among these, the phosphorylation of threonine 1135 (T1135) has been shown to be responsive to growth factors via S6K1. RICTOR is a subunit of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2), which includes mTOR, GβL, RICTOR, and mSIN1. mTOR is a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase that regulates cell growth and proliferation. It exists in two distinct complexes: mTORC1 and mTORC2. Unlike mTORC1, mTORC2 is not directly inhibited by rapamycin. RICTOR, as a key component of mTORC2, facilitates the phosphorylation of Akt/protein kinase B (PKB) at serine 473 (SER473), which activates Akt/PKB. Dysregulation of Akt/PKB has been implicated in cancer and diabetes. Additionally, RICTOR and mTORC2 play critical roles in embryonic growth and development, potentially through their regulation of actin cytoskeleton organization. The expression of RICTOR can be activated by FoxO transcription factors. FoxO has been shown to inhibit mTORC1 while simultaneously activating Akt through the upregulation of RICTOR. Perifosine, a therapeutic agent, has been demonstrated to interfere with mTOR activity by degrading its components, including RICTOR. RICTOR interacts with various proteins and plays roles in several cellular processes. Mutations in the RICTOR gene have been associated with diseases such as foramen magnum meningioma and syringomyelia. Activation of Akt/PKB by RICTOR is also involved in glucose metabolism, mediating both glucose and lipid metabolism. Consequently, the influence of RICTOR and mTORC2 on Akt signaling has been linked to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. In cancer, activation of Akt/PKB promotes cell proliferation and survival. Overactivation of the Akt/PKB pathway by mTORC2, including RICTOR, has been implicated in oncogenesis. In human colorectal carcinoma, RICTOR has been shown to associate with FBXW7 (outside of mTORC2) to mediate the ubiquitination of growth-promoting factors such as cyclin E and c-Myc. Elevated growth factor signaling may suppress the ubiquitinating action of the RICTOR-FBXW7 complex, leading to the accumulation of cyclin E and c-Myc, which drives cell cycle progression. In glioblastoma (GBM), RICTOR, along with EGFR, has been identified as a potential therapeutic target for silencing RNA strategies, which reduce cell proliferation. Co-silencing of RICTOR and EGFR increases sensitivity to alkaloids and alkylating agents. In one PTEN-mutant cell line, co-silencing resulted in tumor eradication. RICTOR is also significantly overexpressed in well-differentiated leiomyosarcomas, where it may influence actin polymerization, allowing transcription and subsequent differentiation in muscle cells. Both RICTOR and RAPTOR, subunits of mTOR, exhibit increased expression in pituitary adenomas, with expression levels correlating with tumor staging. This suggests that mTOR, RAPTOR, and RICTOR are significantly associated with the growth and invasion of pituitary adenomas and may hold predictive and prognostic value in affected patients.
